title: How do you structure a framework's folders (`tests/ pages/ fixtures/ utils/ data/ config/ api/ reports/`) and justify WHY each exists for maintainability and scalability rather than just listing them?
shortTitle: Structuring a framework's folders and justifying why each exists
keyPoints: tests/ holds thin specs expressing intent, separate so the scenario reads clearly and volume can grow without entangling interaction detail
pages/ holds Page Objects with stable locators and interaction methods, so a UI change is a single edit that leaves every spec untouched
fixtures/ holds dependency injection and lifecycle, so setup and teardown are defined once and injected automatically
api/ holds backend helpers for fast preconditions and source-of-truth verification, separate from UI concerns
data/ and config/ externalize inputs and environment settings so the suite is portable and secrets stay out of code
The value is not the folder names but the reasoning: each folder isolates one concern so changes are localized, code is reused, and the structure is self-documenting

s1_definition.oneliner: Each folder isolates one responsibility, tests for intent, pages for UI encapsulation, fixtures for setup and injection, utils for shared logic, data for externalized inputs, config for environment settings, api for backend preconditions, and reports for output, so changes stay localized and the framework scales.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **tests/** – Thin specs expressing what is being verified, separate so scenarios read clearly and volume grows without entangling interaction detail.
- **pages/** – Page Objects with stable locators and interaction methods, so a UI change is a single edit that leaves specs untouched.
- **fixtures/** – Dependency injection and lifecycle logic, so setup and teardown are defined once and injected automatically.
- **utils/** – Cross-cutting UI-agnostic helpers like formatting, random data, and custom assertions.
- **data/** – Externalized test data in JSON, CSV, or factories, so inputs are not hard-coded and can be isolated per worker.
- **config/** – Environment and runner settings so the suite is portable across environments.
- **api/** – Backend helpers for fast preconditions and source-of-truth verification, separate from UI concerns.
- **reports/** – Generated output and artifacts in a known location for CI to publish (gitignored).
s1_definition.analogy: Organizing the National Bank of India automation is like organizing a well-run bank building. The tests folder is the list of daily checks. The pages folder is the directory of specialist clerks who operate each screen. The fixtures folder is the front-desk setup. The utils folder is the shared toolroom. The data folder is the file cabinet of sample customers. The config folder is the rulebook saying which branch to use. The api folder is the fast internal back-channel. And the reports folder is where end-of-day summaries are kept. Each room has one clear purpose, so anyone can find things and a change in one room does not disturb the others.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Folder Structure with Responsibilities
  ───────────────────────────────────────

  framework/
  │
  ├── tests/           WHAT to verify (thin specs)
  │   ├── transfer.spec.ts
  │   ├── loan.spec.ts
  │   └── auth.setup.ts
  │
  ├── pages/           HOW to interact (POs)
  │   ├── TransferPage.ts
  │   └── LoanPage.ts
  │
  ├── components/      SHARED UI parts
  │   ├── HeaderComponent.ts
  │   └── DatePickerComponent.ts
  │
  ├── fixtures/        SETUP + INJECTION
  │   └── bankFixtures.ts
  │
  ├── utils/           SHARED LOGIC
  │   ├── moneyFormatter.ts
  │   └── randomData.ts
  │
  ├── api/             BACKEND HELPERS
  │   └── ApiHelper.ts
  │
  ├── data/            TEST INPUTS
  │   └── loan-test-cases.json
  │
  ├── config/          ENVIRONMENT
  │   └── playwright.config.ts
  │
  ├── .auth/           STORAGE STATE (gitignored)
  │   └── teller.json
  │
  └── reports/         OUTPUT (gitignored)
      └── index.html
```

```text
  Why Each Folder Exists
  ──────────────────────

  Folder     │ Responsibility          │ Change Localized To
  ───────────┼─────────────────────────┼──────────────────────
  tests/     │ Intent + assertions     │ Business logic change
  pages/     │ Locators + interaction  │ UI redesign
  fixtures/  │ Setup + teardown        │ Lifecycle change
  utils/     │ Shared helpers          │ Formatting rule
  api/       │ Backend preconditions   │ API contract change
  data/      │ Test inputs             │ Data scenario change
  config/    │ Environment settings    │ New environment
  reports/   │ Generated diagnostics   │ Reporter change
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
I structure an automation framework so that each folder owns exactly one responsibility, and the value is the reasoning behind each boundary, not the list of names. Tests hold thin specs for readability. Pages hold Page Objects for single-point locator maintenance. Fixtures hold dependency injection for consistent, reusable setup. Utils hold shared helpers so logic lives once. API helpers create fast, reliable preconditions and verify at the source of truth. Data externalizes inputs for portability. Config externalizes environment settings so the suite runs anywhere. And reports hold generated diagnostics for CI to publish.

This structure gives three scaling properties: changes are localized because a UI change touches pages and an environment change touches config; code is reused because shared logic sits in utils, api, and fixtures instead of being copied; and the layout is self-documenting so a new engineer instantly knows where everything belongs.

At the National Bank of India this structure let the suite grow past several hundred tests without becoming unmaintainable. When we added a new environment we only edited config, when a screen was redesigned we only edited pages, and when we needed faster setup we added API seeding without touching specs.

Remember one sentence: each folder isolates one concern so changes are localized, code is reused, and the structure is self-documenting, which is what makes a framework scalable.
